# Treatment definition {#sec-treatment}

We exploit two natural experiments arising from the staggered creation and reclassification of protected areas during the ROR survey period.

## Marovoay / Ankarafantsika (2003) {#sec-treat-maro}

The Ankarafantsika National Park was formally reclassified by Decree 2002-798 on 7 August 2002, merging the former *Réserve Naturelle Intégrale* (60,500 ha, 1927) with forest reserves into a 136,500 ha national park under IUCN Category II. We set the treatment year to **2003** — the first full ROR survey year following the decree.^[Using 2002 as the treatment onset instead has negligible impact on the estimated ATT.]

The Marovoay observatory comprises four *fokontany* split by the Betsiboka River:

| Fokontany | Bank | Distance to PA | Role | Treatment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bepako | East | 5.2 km | Treated | From 2003 |
| Madiromiongana | East | 11.7 km | Treated | From 2003 |
| Ampijoroa | West | 3.5 km (road) / ~18.5 km (effective) | Donor | Never |
| Maroala | West | 5.8 km (road) / ~20.8 km (effective) | Donor | Never |

: Marovoay site treatment assignments. {#tbl-maro-sites}

The Betsiboka River constitutes a natural treatment barrier. Although the west-bank sites are geographically close to the park, the river makes direct access costly — effectively adding ~15 km of travel. The 2025 resurvey confirms this: 38% of east-bank households report visiting Ankarafantsika, versus 15% on the west bank. East-bank households also report the park as a source of food (23% vs 8%) and wood (24% vs 12%).

## Alaotra / Lac Alaotra (2008) {#sec-treat-ala}

The Lac Alaotra new protected area (425 km², IUCN Category VI) was created in stages: a temporary protection decree in 2007, followed by intensified CBNRM enforcement by Durrell Wildlife Conservation Trust from approximately 2008. We set the treatment year to **2008**.

Unlike Marovoay, no natural boundary creates differential exposure within the Alaotra observatory. The 2025 resurvey shows uniform PA interaction rates (37–54%) across all hamlets, reflecting the lake-marsh ecosystem's central role in all communities' livelihoods. We therefore treat the **entire observatory as a single treated unit**, aggregated to a site-level mean.

## Extensions (2006–2007) {#sec-treat-ext}

Three additional observatory–PA pairs provide shorter treatment windows (see [Chapter 5](05_extensions.qmd)):

- **Farafangana / CFAV** (IUCN VI, 2006) — Corridor Forestier Ambositra-Vondrozo
- **Toliara North / Amoron'i Onilahy** (IUCN VI, 2007)
- **Fénérive East / Tampolo** (IUCN IV, 2007) — coastal forest reserve

# Donor pool selection {#sec-donor-pool}

The generalized synthetic control method requires that donor units be **unexposed to treatment**. We start with 9 donor observatories (Antsirabe, Antsohihy, Tsiroanomandidy, Farafangana, Ambovombe, Toliara North, Fénérive East, Mahanoro, Itasy), providing approximately 60 donor sites.

A systematic spatial audit ([Appendix B](A2_donor_validity.qmd)) checks whether these donors are themselves adjacent to active PAs during the study period. Using a dynamic WDPA layer that records when each PA became legally operative, we flag any donor commune within 20 km of an active PA boundary as **contaminated**.

| Status | Observatories | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **Clean** | Antsirabe (02), Tsiroanomandidy (13), Ambovombe (16), Mahanoro (25), Itasy (41) | No active PA within 20 km during 1999–2014 |
| **Contaminated** | Antsohihy (12), Farafangana (15), Toliara North (23), Fénérive East (24) | PA created within 20 km during study period |

: Donor pool PA exposure classification. {#tbl-donor-status}

The main results use the full 9-donor pool; robustness checks ([Appendix C](A3_robustness.qmd)) confirm that restricting to the 5 clean donors does not materially change the estimates. In the extension analysis ([Chapter 5](05_extensions.qmd)), the contaminated donors become *treated* units with their own PA exposure — a design feature rather than a threat.

# Generalized synthetic control {#sec-gsynth}

We use the generalized synthetic control method (gsynth) of @Xu2017 to estimate treatment effects. For each treated unit $i$ in post-treatment period $t$, gsynth models the outcome as:

$$
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \xi_t + \boldsymbol{\lambda}_i' \boldsymbol{f}_t + D_{it} \cdot \delta_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

where $\alpha_i$ are unit fixed effects, $\xi_t$ are time fixed effects, $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i$ are unit-specific factor loadings, $\boldsymbol{f}_t$ are common time factors, and $D_{it}$ is the treatment indicator. The interactive fixed effects ($\boldsymbol{\lambda}_i' \boldsymbol{f}_t$) relax the parallel trends assumption by allowing units to follow heterogeneous time paths driven by unobserved factors.

Key implementation choices:

- **Unit of analysis** — site-level (*fokontany*) medians of log equivalised income. The rotating panel design makes household-level panel estimation unreliable; site-level aggregation preserves cross-sectional representativeness.
- **Factor selection** — leave-one-out cross-validation over $r \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$.
- **Inference** — parametric bootstrap with 200 replications.
- **Minimum pre-treatment periods** — $\text{min.T0} = 3$ to ensure adequate pre-treatment fit.

We estimate **two separate models**: one for Marovoay (2 treated sites, ~60 donors) and one for Alaotra (1 treated unit, ~60 donors). The Alaotra model reduces to an interactive fixed-effects synthetic control with a single treated unit.

## Inference with few treated units {#sec-inference}

A fundamental constraint is the small number of treated units: 2 sites for Marovoay, 1 for Alaotra. With so few clusters, conventional asymptotic inference is unreliable.

For Marovoay, a Fisher permutation test over the 4 observable sites (2 treated among 4) yields $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ possible allocations, so the **minimum achievable p-value** is $1/6 \approx 0.167$. When Alaotra sites are included as additional donors, this falls to $1/\binom{7}{2} \approx 0.048$.

We report bootstrap confidence intervals and p-values but interpret them in light of this power ceiling. Failure to reject the null at conventional thresholds reflects design constraints, not necessarily absence of an effect. Placebo-in-space tests ([Appendix C](A3_robustness.qmd)) provide complementary evidence on the uniqueness of estimated effects.

# Towards household-level DiD {#sec-did-roadmap}

The gsynth approach is well-suited to the current data but has an important limitation: it operates at the site level, discarding within-site household heterogeneity. The 2026 survey wave will enable a richer design:

- **Callaway–Sant'Anna DiD** at the household level, exploiting four staggered treatment cohorts (Ankarafantsika 2003, Farafangana/Toliara/Fénérive 2006–07, Alaotra 2008, plus never-treated).
- **Not-yet-treated controls** — Alaotra households observed in 2003–2007 (before their own treatment) serve as additional controls for the Ankarafantsika cohort.
- **Household covariates** for conditional parallel trends (demographics, pre-treatment income, agricultural dependence).
- **Sun–Abraham event studies** via `fixest::sunab()` as a complementary estimator.

This forward-looking design is discussed further in [Chapter 6](06_discussion.qmd).
